title: Denarius of Tiberius (the 'tribute penny')
summary: A silver coin about 19 mm across and 1.5 mm thick, weighing roughly 3.8–3.9 g. The relief here is schematic — the proportions are what the model is for; see the photograph on the Insights card for the real portrait.

title: Alabastron — the perfume flask
summary: A calcite flask of the classic shape: rounded base (it was stood in a ring or held), narrow neck, and a flat disc lip for wiping the last drop across the skin. Mark says the woman 'broke' it — snapping the sealed neck. The height modelled here (18 cm) is a typical size; the Gospels give no dimensions, and a Roman pound of nard (John 12:3) would need a flask towards the larger end of the range.

title: Tyrian shekel (tetradrachm) — the temple's silver
summary: The coin the temple tax had to be paid in: about 26 mm across, 3 mm thick, 14 g of high-grade silver — four times a denarius. Obverse: head of the god Melqart-Heracles; reverse: an eagle with the legend ΤΥΡΟΥ ΙΕΡΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΑΣΥΛΟΥ, 'of Tyre, holy and inviolable'. The stater in the fish's mouth (Matthew 17:27) was one of these; Judas's thirty pieces may have been.

title: The widow's two lepta
summary: The smallest coins in Judea. Mark calls the widow's gift lepta duo, 'two lepta', and explains it to Roman readers as a kodrantēs (quadrans), 1/64 of a denarius; Luke 12:59's 'very last penny' is the same coin. The Gospels do not say whose coins hers were. The ones most found in the excavated levels of the 1st century AD are the bronzes of the Hasmonean king Alexander Jannaeus (103–76 BC), struck a century and more earlier and still in use: an anchor, hung upside down as on a ship's side, with the Greek 'of King Alexander', and on the other side an eight-rayed star. They were struck on small, ragged flans, often off-centre, and vary widely: specimens of the type in the American Numismatic Society weigh from about 0.5 g to 3.6 g, the smallest sort (the anchor within a circle) mostly 0.8–1.8 g. The left coin is drawn at the size of one in the Yale University Art Gallery, minted in Jerusalem: 15.9 mm across, 1.87 g. The right is one of the smaller sort, turned to show its star. Its size, the thickness of both and the relief are estimates, each saying what it rests on in the list under the model.

title: Ark of the covenant — built as the text describes it
summary: Read or play Exodus 25:10–22 (the instructions) or 37:1–9 (Bezalel making it) and the ark builds up verse by verse: the acacia chest, its gold overlay and molding, the rings, the poles, the Testimony, the mercy seat, and the cherubim with their wings. Elsewhere it is shown whole. The text gives only the chest (2½ × 1½ × 1½ cubits) and the cover (2½ × 1½); the metric size assumes a common cubit of ≈44.5 cm. Everything else, from the cover's thickness to the look of the cherubim, is reconstructed; each estimate says what it rests on, both at the step that adds it and in the list under the model.

title: The tabernacle and its courtyard — built as the text describes it
summary: Read or play through the tabernacle chapters and it goes up as they describe it. There are three accounts: the instructions (Exodus 25–30, furniture first, then the tent, then the court), Bezalel's making of it (36–38, tent first), and Moses setting it up (40:17–33, from the bases upward). In chapters 28–29, on the priests, it stays as far as the instructions have got. Everywhere else it is shown whole. The text gives the court (100 × 50 cubits, hangings 5 high), the frames (10 × 1½), the curtains and most furniture sizes, and the model follows those. Where the tent stands in the court, how thick the frames were, the outer coverings, the basin and the pattern of the weaving are all reconstructed; each estimate says what it rests on, both at the step that adds it and in the list under the model. Use Show outside / Show inside to see the whole tent or cut it open to see the furniture.

estimates.lampstand-shaft-cups: four cups on the shaft: one low down, 5–6 handbreadths up, and three at the top, as b. Menachot 28b places them
estimates.lampstand-lamps: the lamps' shape is not given; small oil lamps are drawn, spouts turned north toward the table so they 'illuminate the area in front of it' (25:37)
estimates.lampstand-tools: wick trimmers and trays of no stated size, set down beside the base
estimates.linen: ten curtains of 28 × 4 make a cover 40 long and 28 across, so it hangs 9 cubits down each side and 10 down the back. The colours are in the text; the banded pattern is not, and the woven cherubim are not drawn
estimates.goat-hair: eleven curtains of 30 × 4, reaching the ground on each side (26:13); the sixth is folded double over the front (26:9)
estimates.ram-skins: no size is given; drawn over the roof and down the sides
estimates.leather: no size is given; drawn over the roof only. The animal behind 'fine leather' (tachash) is disputed
estimates.frames-south: frames are 10 × 1½ cubits (26:16); their thickness is not given, and ½ cubit is assumed for every wall
estimates.bases-south: two silver bases per frame (26:19); their size is not given
estimates.frames-west: six frames plus two corner frames (26:22-23); how the corners were joined is disputed, so the eight are drawn spread evenly across the back wall
estimates.bars: five bars a wall (26:26-27). The middle bar runs end to end through the frames (26:28) but is drawn on the outside so it can be seen; the other four are assumed to be half-length
estimates.veil: hung from the clasps (26:33). Five curtains of 4 cubits come to 20 cubits, which leaves a Most Holy Place 10 cubits square. That is derived from the curtain sizes, not stated
estimates.altar-body: 5 × 5 × 3 cubits of acacia, hollow, made of boards (27:8), so it is drawn open at top and bottom. The text does not say where in the court it stood; it is placed in the eastern half, between the basin and the gate

estimates.altar-utensils: pots, shovels, sprinkling bowls, meat forks and firepans (27:3), one of each, of no stated size

title: Noah's ark — built as the text describes it
summary: Read or play Genesis 6:14–16 and the ark builds up as God describes it to Noah: the gopher-wood hull, its rooms and its coat of pitch, then the roof, the door in the side and the three decks. Elsewhere it is shown whole. The text gives the size (300 × 50 × 30 cubits), and the model follows it. The metric size assumes a common cubit of ≈44.5 cm; the Ark Encounter's full-size replica in Kentucky uses a longer royal cubit of 51.8 cm, which makes it ≈155 m long. The hull's volume, 450,000 cubic cubits (≈40,000 m³ on the common cubit), is worked out from those figures, not stated. The shape, the rooms, the deck heights and the door are reconstructed; each estimate says what it rests on, both at the step that adds it and in the list under the model. Use Show outside / Show inside to see the whole hull or cut it open to see the decks.

steps.basis: the size in v. 15 is already built into the hull at v. 14

estimates.hull: tevah means 'a box' (the same word is used for the basket of Moses, Exod 2:3), and the text gives only length, width and height, so it is drawn as a rectangular barge. Tim Lovett's design for Answers in Genesis, whose Ark Encounter is a full-size replica, gives it a ship's hull instead, with a wind-catching bow and a skeg at the stern for seaworthiness; the text supports neither over the other. Wall thickness is not given; ½ cubit is assumed
estimates.pitch: kopher is a coating, usually taken as bitumen; drawn as a dark skin over the hull inside and out
estimates.rooms: qinnim, literally 'nests'; their number, size and layout are not given. Drawn as a room every 15 cubits either side of a 10-cubit central aisle, the partitions running through all three decks
estimates.roof: the BSB reads tsohar as 'roof' and has the walls finished a cubit below it, so the roof is drawn on posts leaving a cubit-high opening all round. Others read tsohar as 'light' or 'window': Rashi gives both a window and a sloping roof narrowing to a cubit at the top, and Lovett's design has a skylight down the middle of the roof, a 'noon light' that 'ends a cubit upward and above'. Drawn in bare wood; whether it was pitched is not said
estimates.door: 'in the side', with no size or deck given; drawn 6 × 8 cubits, midway along the lower deck
estimates.decks: three decks, the lowest being the hull floor; their heights are not given, so they are drawn equal, 10 cubits each. Rashi, after b. Sanhedrin 108b, puts people on the top deck, animals in the middle and refuse at the bottom

title: Solomon's temple — built as the text describes it
summary: Read or play 1 Kings 6–8 or 2 Chronicles 3–5 and the temple goes up as each account describes it. Kings builds the house first: walls, porch, windows, side chambers, roof, cedar panelling, gold, cherubim and doors. Then come Huram's bronzes (the pillars, the Sea and the stands), then the gold furnishings, and last the ark. Chronicles is shorter. It leaves out the side chambers and windows, and it adds a veil and the great bronze altar. Kings names one golden table, Chronicles ten; the model has ten, and in Kings only one appears. Elsewhere the temple is shown whole. The text gives the house (60 × 20 × 30 cubits), the porch, the three storeys of side chambers (5, 6 and 7 cubits wide), the inner sanctuary (a 20-cubit cube), the cherubim, the pillars, the Sea, the stands and the altar, and the model follows those. The metric size assumes a common cubit of ≈44.5 cm. Chronicles measures 'according to the old standard' (2 Chr 3:3), which is often taken to be the longer royal cubit of ≈52 cm; on that cubit the house would be ≈31 m long. Wall thicknesses, doorways, the court and most placements are reconstructed. Each estimate says what it rests on, both at the step that adds it and in the list under the model. The carvings of gourds, flowers, palms and cherubim, the lions and oxen on the stands and the smaller vessels are not drawn. Use Show outside / Show inside to see the whole house or cut it open to see the furniture. The temple also changes after it is built. Ahaz moves the bronze altar, strips the stands and sets the Sea down on stone; Hezekiah strips the gold from the doors; the Babylonians break up the bronzes, carry off the furnishings and burn the house. Read or play those passages and the temple changes verse by verse as they tell it; anywhere else, the buttons under the model show it as it was after each.

states.label: Ahaz (≈ 732 BC)
states.basis: after meeting Tiglath-pileser at Damascus, Ahaz has Uriah build an altar copied from one he saw there and moves the bronze altar to its north (16:10-14). He cuts off the stands' panels, takes down their basins, and sets the Sea down from the oxen onto a stone base (16:17). The date is Damascus's fall to Assyria, which the Assyrian records put in 732 BC. The oxen are not mentioned again, so they are taken away here. 2 Chr 28:24 adds that he cut up the temple's vessels and shut its doors, which the model does not show

states.label: Hezekiah (701 BC)
states.basis: in his fourteenth year, when Sennacherib invaded (701 BC by the Assyrian annals), Hezekiah strips the gold from the temple's doors and doorposts to pay the tribute (18:16). The text says it was gold 'he had plated', perhaps when he repaired the doors (2 Chr 29:3). Ahaz's changes are still in place; Hezekiah's reforms (2 Kgs 18:4, 2 Chr 29) do not say he undid them

states.label: Babylon (587/586 BC)
states.basis: Nebuzaradan burns the house (2 Kgs 25:9). The Chaldeans break up the pillars, the stands and the Sea and carry the bronze to Babylon, with the vessels of bronze, gold and silver (25:13-17; Jer 52:17-23), 'everything… both large and small' (2 Chr 36:18). What burned or was taken is removed in the order each account gives it. The wood and gold of the house go with the fire. The bronze altar goes with 'all the articles of bronze', which do not name it. The stone walls, the side chambers, the court and Ahaz's stone altar are left standing, because the text does not say they were torn down and it does not say how much of them survived the fire. The ark's fate is not recorded in Kings or Chronicles; it is not seen again, so it is drawn going with the house

estimates.walls: the text gives the interior (60 × 20 × 30) but not the walls' thickness. They are drawn 6 cubits thick, the figure Ezekiel's temple gives (Ezek 41:5), stepping in a cubit at each storey of the side chambers so their beams rest on the ledges (6:6). The main doorway is drawn 10 cubits wide, as Ezekiel's is (41:2), and 15 high, which is not given
estimates.portico: 20 across and 10 deep (1 Kgs 6:3). Its height is 20 in the BSB of 2 Chr 3:4, following some Greek and Syriac manuscripts; the Hebrew text reads 120. It is drawn open to the east
estimates.windows: 'narrow windows framed high' (6:4). The Hebrew is often read as windows narrowing inward, or latticed. Their number and size are not given; slots are drawn every 5 cubits above the side chambers
estimates.side-chambers: the widths of the three storeys (5, 6 and 7) and their height (5 each) are in the text (6:6, 10). The outer wall's 5 cubits follow Ezek 41:9, and the floors are assumed to be a cubit thick. The individual rooms are not drawn. The 'Ain Dara temple in Syria has a similar corridor of rooms round three sides
estimates.stairs: the Hebrew lulim is read as a winding stair or as trapdoors. Drawn as a spiral just inside the south door, whose size and place along the wall are not given
estimates.roof: cedar beams and planks (6:9). Drawn flat, as the text gives no pitch
estimates.partition: the inner sanctuary is 20 high (6:20) inside a house 30 high. It is drawn with a lower ceiling and an upper room above it (2 Chr 3:9 mentions upper rooms); some reconstructions raise its floor instead. The doorway is drawn 6 wide, as in Ezek 41:3, and 10 high
estimates.chains: 'across the front of the inner sanctuary' (6:21); drawn as two swags above its doorway. Their length and number are not given
estimates.cherubim: 10 high, of olive wood (6:23); the text gives no form. They stand on their feet facing the main room (2 Chr 3:13), so they are drawn as schematic standing figures
estimates.cherubim-wings: each wing is 5 cubits, and together the four span the room's 20, touching both walls and each other in the middle (6:24-27). Their height and shape are not given; they are drawn level at the shoulder
estimates.inner-doors: 'five-sided doorposts' (6:31) may instead mean a doorway a fifth of the wall's width. The doors are drawn standing open, since 8:8 says the ark's poles could be seen from the hall
estimates.doors: two doors of two folding leaves each (6:34), filling the 10-cubit doorway; drawn closed
estimates.veil: Chronicles has both a veil (3:14) and doors to the inner sanctuary (4:22) but does not say how they hung together. The veil is drawn just inside the doorway
estimates.court: 'three rows of dressed stone and one row of trimmed cedar beams' (6:36) is drawn as three courses a cubit high with cedar on top. The court's size is not given; it is drawn to leave room round the house for the altar, the Sea and the stands. Ezekiel's inner court is 100 cubits square (Ezek 40:47)
estimates.pillars: 18 high and 12 round (1 Kgs 7:15; Jer 52:21), so ≈3.8 across; Jeremiah adds that they were hollow, four fingers thick. 2 Chr 3:15 gives 35 cubits, often read as the two together. Whether they stood free or held up the porch roof is disputed. With 5-cubit capitals they come to 23, taller than the 20-cubit porch, so they are drawn standing free in front of it
estimates.capitals: 5 high (7:16; Jer 52:22). 2 Kgs 25:17 gives 3, perhaps not counting the lily-work. The form is inferred from 'bowl-shaped' (7:41) and 'shaped like lilies… four cubits' (7:19)
estimates.networks: lattice over each bowl and 'seven wreaths of chainwork' (7:17); the pattern is not given
estimates.pomegranates: two rows round each capital, 400 in all (7:42), so 100 a row. 2 Chr 3:16 gives a hundred; Jer 52:23 has 96 'on the sides' and 100 in all
estimates.sea: 10 across, 5 high and 30 round, a handbreadth thick with a lily-shaped brim (7:23-26). Measured across a circle 10 wide, the line should be ≈31.4, not 30. Drawn with the line round the body just below a brim that flares to the full 10, which is one common reading; another is that the 30 was measured inside the handbreadth-thick wall. The bowl's profile is not given. Drawn this way it holds ≈24.5 m³, about 1,100 baths of ≈22 litres. Kings says 2,000 baths and Chronicles 3,000, which would need a smaller bath or a fuller, more cylindrical vessel
estimates.sea-ornaments: two rows of gourds, ten to the cubit (7:24), so 300 a row round the 30-cubit line. Chronicles has 'figures of oxen' (2 Chr 4:3), probably from the similar Hebrew word for oxen (bakar) and gourds (peka'im)
estimates.oxen: their size is not given; drawn about life size, so the Sea stands 2.4 cubits off the ground. Schematic figures
estimates.stands: 4 × 4 × 3 (7:27). The 3 is taken to include the wheels. The supports and the handles (7:30, 34) are not drawn; each stand is corner uprights with the round band on top (7:35). Placed in a row on each side of the house (7:39); their spacing is not given
estimates.stand-panels: the panels between the uprights (7:28), drawn plain; their lions, oxen, cherubim and wreaths (7:29, 36) are not drawn
estimates.door-gold: 'gold hammered evenly over the carvings' (6:35) is drawn as a gold panel on each leaf
estimates.great-altar: Ahaz's altar, copied from one in Damascus (2 Kgs 16:10-11), is called 'the great altar' (16:15), but no size, material or form is given. It is drawn in stone, 14 × 14 × 7 cubits. It stands east of the bronze altar, which was 'between the new altar and the house' (16:14)
estimates.bronze-altar-north: the bronze altar moved 'to the north side of the new altar' (16:14), drawn without the ramp, which is itself an estimate
estimates.sea-on-stone: 'a stone base' (16:17) is the Hebrew for a pavement of stones. Drawn as a low platform a cubit high, since its size is not given
estimates.stand-wheels: a cubit and a half across (7:32), on axles, like chariot wheels (7:33); drawn as solid discs
estimates.basins: 4 cubits across, holding 40 baths (7:38). The depth is not given; a shallow bowl 1.4 cubits deep holds ≈900 litres, which is 40 baths of ≈22 litres. That depth is worked out from those figures, not stated
estimates.bronze-altar: 20 × 20 × 10 (2 Chr 4:1); drawn as a plain block with horns. The text does not say how priests reached a top 10 cubits up (Exod 20:26 forbids steps). A ramp is drawn on the south, 32 × 16 cubits, the size Mishnah Middot 3:3 gives for the Second Temple's altar. Placed on the axis in front of the porch; 2 Kgs 16:14 has it 'before the LORD… at the front of the temple'
estimates.incense-altar: shown as the tabernacle's (1 × 1 × 2, Exod 30:2); the size of Solomon's is not given
estimates.lampstands: each is shown as the tabernacle's lampstand; the text does not describe Solomon's beyond 'pure gold'. 'Five on the right side and five on the left' (7:49) is drawn as a row along each wall of the main hall, right being south
estimates.table: each table is shown as the tabernacle's (2 × 1 × 1½). Kings' one table is drawn in the middle of the north row, where the tabernacle's stood (Exod 26:35)
estimates.more-tables: Chronicles' ten (2 Chr 4:8), 'five on the south side and five on the north', are drawn in rows between the lampstands
estimates.ark: shown as the Ark of the covenant card builds it, beneath the middle of the cherubim's wings (8:6-7), its poles running east–west. 8:8 says the poles' ends could be seen from the Holy Place; the model's poles, ≈4½ cubits long, would not reach the doorway. b. Yoma 54a says they pressed out against the curtain 'like the two breasts of a woman'

title: The high priest's garments — made as the text describes them
summary: Read or play Exodus 28 (the instructions) or 39:1–31 (the making) and the garments are made verse by verse: the ephod and its shoulder pieces, the onyx stones, the breastpiece and its twelve stones row by row, the rings, chains and blue cord that hold it, the blue robe with its bells and pomegranates, the gold plate, and finally the tunic, turban, sash and undergarments. Leviticus 8:7–9 gives a third order, the one Moses dresses Aaron in, from the tunic outward. Elsewhere they are shown whole. The only measure in the text is the breastpiece, a span (½ cubit, ≈22 cm) square when folded double. They are worn by the size figure (≈1.66 m), whom the other models have standing beside them. Every other shape and size is reconstructed from Josephus, the Talmud and Rashi; each says what it rests on, both at the step that adds it and in the list under the model. Aaron's sons' tunics, sashes and headbands (28:40) are not drawn.

steps.basis: the settings of v. 11 and the fastening on the shoulders of v. 12 are drawn with the stones
these chains are taken to be the ones fastened to the breastpiece at vv. 22-25, so they hang from the shoulder settings to where it will be
its size, a span square folded double, is in v. 16
the plate is tied to the front of the turban, which is only made at v. 39

omits.urim-and-thummim: the account of the making does not mention them; Moses puts them in the breastpiece at Lev 8:8

omits.undergarments: the dressing does not mention them; Exod 28:42-43 and Lev 16:4 have them worn under the tunic

steps.basis: one verse puts on the tunic, the sash, the robe and the ephod, and ties the ephod's band, so all four appear together

estimates.ephod-apron: the text gives the materials but not the shape. Drawn after Rashi on 28:6: an apron like a riding apron, tied on behind at the height of the heart, as wide as the back and reaching to the heels. Josephus (Ant. 3.7.5) instead makes it a short coat a cubit deep, with sleeves. The pattern of the gold and coloured threads is not given
estimates.shoulder-pieces: Rashi has them rise from the band behind, over the shoulders, and hang a little below them in front; they are drawn down the front to just above the band, so the rings of 28:27 can sit at their foot
estimates.waistband: of one piece with the ephod (28:8); drawn a handbreadth wide, at the height of the heart (Rashi). Its width is not given
estimates.onyx-stones: shoham is uncertain (Strong's: 'probably the beryl'); drawn as dark onyx in round gold settings. Josephus calls them sardonyxes (Ant. 3.7.5). Their size is not given
estimates.chains: braided gold cord (28:14, 22); their length is not given, so they run from the shoulder settings straight to the breastpiece's top corners
estimates.breastpiece-pouch: a span square 'when folded over double' (28:16), so it is drawn as a pouch ½ cubit square; the span is taken as half the cubit. Its thickness is not given
estimates.stones-row-1: odem, pitdah, bareqet: the BSB's ruby, topaz and emerald. The Hebrew gem names are uncertain (Strong's: 'the ruby, garnet, or some other red gem'; 'probably the topaz'; 'perhaps the emerald'), so the colours follow the BSB's names. Their size is not given, and the tribes' names engraved on them (28:21) are not drawn
estimates.stones-row-2: nofekh, sappir, yahalom: the BSB's turquoise, sapphire and diamond. Strong's has 'probably the garnet', 'probably the sapphire' and 'probably onyx'; many take sappir to be lapis lazuli, and a diamond could hardly have been engraved with a name. Colours follow the BSB
estimates.stones-row-3: leshem, shevo, achlamah: the BSB's jacinth, agate and amethyst; Strong's has 'perhaps the jacinth', 'probably the agate', 'probably the amethyst'. Colours follow the BSB
estimates.stones-row-4: tarshish, shoham, yashfeh: the BSB's beryl, onyx and jasper; Strong's has 'perhaps the topaz', 'probably the beryl', and jasper 'from the resemblance in name'. Colours follow the BSB
estimates.lower-rings: 'on the inside edge next to the ephod' (28:26): drawn on the back face at the bottom corners
estimates.ephod-rings: 'at the bottom of the two shoulder pieces… near its seam just above its woven waistband' (28:27)
estimates.blue-cord: its length is not given; drawn as a short tie between the rings, so the breastpiece 'does not swing out' (28:28)
estimates.urim-and-thummim: the text never says what they were, only that they were put 'in' the breastpiece (28:30); drawn as two small plain lots standing in its fold
estimates.robe-body: 'entirely of blue' (28:31) and woven in one piece (39:22). Josephus (Ant. 3.7.4) has it reach the feet, parted for the arms; it is drawn to the ankles, with the tunic showing below it
estimates.robe-collar: a woven binding round the opening 'so that it will not tear' (28:32); drawn as a thick band
estimates.pomegranates: the text gives no number; b. Zevachim 88b says thirty-six on each side, seventy-two in all (Rabbi Dosa says thirty-six bells in all). Drawn alternating with the bells, in turn blue, purple and scarlet, about a centimetre across
estimates.bells: seventy-two after b. Zevachim 88b, alternating with the pomegranates (28:34). Their size is not given
estimates.plate: two fingerbreadths wide, running round the forehead from ear to ear (b. Shabbat 63b). Its inscription, HOLY TO THE LORD, is not drawn
estimates.plate-cord: a blue cord ties the plate to the front of the turban (28:37); drawn round the back of the head
estimates.tunic: fine linen woven in a check (tashbets, 28:39; Strong's: 'checkered stuff'). Its length and sleeves follow Josephus (Ant. 3.7.2): 'reaches down to the feet… and has sleeves that are tied fast to the arms'
estimates.turban: fine linen (28:39); its shape and how it was wound are not given. Josephus (Ant. 3.7.6) gives the high priest a second, blue-embroidered layer, which is not drawn
estimates.sash: linen embroidered with blue, purple and scarlet (39:29). After Josephus (Ant. 3.7.2): four fingers broad, wound round the breast a little above the elbows, its ends hanging to the ankles. It is worn under the robe, so only its ends show below the hem; at the steps that make it, the robe and tunic are cut open to show it
estimates.undergarments: linen 'from waist to thigh' (28:42); drawn as short breeches under the tunic, which is cut open, with the robe and ephod, at the steps that make them

title: Ezekiel's temple — measured as the vision describes it
summary: Read or play Ezekiel 40–43 and the temple goes up as the man with the measuring rod walks Ezekiel through it. First comes the wall round the whole, then the east gate piece by piece: threshold, chambers, portico, posts, windows and palm trees. Then come the outer court, the north and south gates, the three gates of the inner court and the tables at the north one. After them the inner court, the temple house with its side rooms and platform, the building to the west and the priests' chambers. Last is the altar (43:13-17). Elsewhere the temple is shown whole. Ezekiel measures in long cubits, 'a cubit and a handbreadth' (40:5; 43:13). The metric size assumes ≈52 cm, a common cubit of ≈44.5 cm plus a handbreadth. Unlike Solomon's temple, this one is given mostly in plan. The lengths and widths add up: along the axis, outer gate 50, court 100, inner gate 50, inner court 100, temple 100 and the yard and west building 100 make the 500 of 42:16-20, with the altar at the centre. Heights are mostly not given. The house, the gates and the chambers are drawn at estimated heights, and the steps each rise 0.6 cubit, worked out from the platform. The gateposts are drawn 60 cubits high, as the BSB reads 40:14, but the Hebrew there is uncertain. In several places (40:44, 48-49) the BSB follows the Greek, and the model follows the BSB. Each estimate says what it rests on, at the step that adds it and in the list under the model. The carved cherubim and palms of the house, the hooks of 40:43 and the kitchens of 46:19-24 are not drawn. Use Show outside / Show inside to open the house. What Ezekiel saw is read in different ways (listed under the model). The model draws the plan as the text gives it; what it stands for is not something it can show.
dimensions: Court 500 × 500 long cubits (≈ 260 m square) · temple 100 × 50 (≈ 52 × 26 m) · gates 50 × 25

steps.basis: the east gate's steps are not counted; the north and south gates have seven (40:22, 26)

estimates.outer-wall: a rod (6 long cubits) thick and a rod high (40:5). The 500 of 42:16-20 is taken as measured round its outside, and each outer gate's threshold, also a rod deep (40:6), as passing through it. The wall's height is counted from the outer court, which the text does not say
estimates.outer-court: the text gives seven steps up to the outer gates (40:22, 26) but not how high they rise. Every step in the model rises 0.6 cubit, the platform's 6 cubits (41:8) shared among the ten steps up to it (40:49). On that rise the outer court stands ≈4 cubits above the ground outside, the inner court ≈9 and the temple's floor 15. The courts are drawn as raised terraces
estimates.pavement: 'corresponded to the length of the gates' (40:18) is taken to make it 50 cubits wide. It is drawn along the three walls that have gates
estimates.outer-chambers: thirty (40:17); their size and arrangement are not given. Drawn as ten along each wall with a gate, five either side of it, each 20 × 10 × 8 cubits
estimates.east-gate-steps: seven steps (40:22, 26), each a cubit deep and rising 0.6 cubit (see the outer court)
estimates.east-gate-chambers: each a rod square, with 5 cubits between them (40:7), three a side (40:10). 40:11 gives the entrance as 10 wide and 'its length' as 13, which is read variously. The passage is drawn 10 wide, with the chambers 6 deep behind it and outer walls 1½ thick, which makes the 25 of 40:13. The six-chambered gates excavated at Megiddo, Hazor and Gezer have the same plan, three chambers either side of the passage
estimates.east-gate-portico: 8 deep with jambs 2 thick (40:9). The walls' height is not given; they are drawn 10 cubits high
estimates.east-gate-roof: 'from the roof of one gate chamber to the roof of the opposite one… twenty-five cubits' (40:13). Roofs are drawn over the chambers and the portico; the passage between the chambers is left open
estimates.east-gate-posts: the meaning of 40:14 is uncertain (JPS). The Hebrew reads 'he made the jambs sixty cubits'. The BSB takes the 60 as their height and is followed here, so the portico's jambs are carried up to 60 cubits (≈31 m). Keil defends that height, likening the posts to church towers grown out of gate pillars. The NIV instead reads 60 as a length measured along the walls, and the JPS as the vestibule's
estimates.east-gate-barriers: 'a wall one cubit high' in front of each chamber (40:12); its thickness is not given
estimates.east-gate-windows: 'beveled windows all around the inside' (40:16); their number and size are not given. A slot is drawn through the back wall of each chamber and of the portico
estimates.east-gate-palms: 'each side pillar was decorated with palm trees' (40:16). The design is not given; a palm is drawn in relief on each pier and jamb, facing the passage
estimates.north-gate: 'the same measurements as the first gate: fifty cubits long and twenty-five cubits wide' (40:21-22), so it is drawn as the east gate is
estimates.south-gate: 'the same measurements as the others' (40:24-26), so it is drawn as the east gate is
estimates.inner-south-gate: 'the same measurements as the others' (40:28-29, 32-33, 35-36), but turned the other way: its portico faces the outer court (40:31, 34, 37) and eight steps lead up to it. It is drawn standing out into the outer court on a base as high as those steps, its threshold at the edge of the inner court, which makes the 100 cubits 'from gateway to gateway' (40:19, 23, 27) and the 100-cubit court (40:47) add up
estimates.inner-east-gate: 'the same measurements as the others' (40:28-29, 32-33, 35-36), but turned the other way: its portico faces the outer court (40:31, 34, 37) and eight steps lead up to it. It is drawn standing out into the outer court on a base as high as those steps, its threshold at the edge of the inner court, which makes the 100 cubits 'from gateway to gateway' (40:19, 23, 27) and the 100-cubit court (40:47) add up
estimates.inner-north-gate: 'the same measurements as the others' (40:28-29, 32-33, 35-36), but turned the other way: its portico faces the outer court (40:31, 34, 37) and eight steps lead up to it. It is drawn standing out into the outer court on a base as high as those steps, its threshold at the edge of the inner court, which makes the 100 cubits 'from gateway to gateway' (40:19, 23, 27) and the 100-cubit court (40:47) add up
estimates.washing-rooms: 'a chamber with a doorway by the portico in each of the inner gateways' (40:38). Their size and side are not given; each is drawn 8 × 6 against the portico
estimates.slaughter-tables: four inside the portico and four outside, by the steps (40:39-41). The text gives their number but not their size, so they are drawn the size of the stone tables (40:42)
estimates.stone-tables: a cubit and a half square and a cubit high (40:42). Where they stood is not given; they are drawn inside the portico, either side of the way through
estimates.priests-rooms: two chambers, for the priests of the temple and of the altar (40:44-46). The BSB's 'south gate' follows the Greek; the Hebrew reads 'east gate', and calls them chambers 'for singers'. Their size and place beside the gates are not given; each is drawn 25 × 10, east of its gate
estimates.inner-court: 100 cubits square (40:47), eight steps above the outer court (40:31). The text describes no wall round it, so its edge is drawn as the edge of a terrace, which runs on behind to hold the temple's yard (the 20 cubits of 41:10)
estimates.temple-portico: 20 wide and 12 deep, with jambs of 5 and walls of 3 either side of an opening of 14 (40:48-49). The 12 and the 14 follow the Greek, as the BSB does; the Hebrew has 11 and lacks the 14 (JPS). Its height is not given; it is drawn as high as the house
estimates.temple-steps: ten steps (40:49), which also follows the Greek; the Hebrew says only 'by steps'. Drawn as wide as the portico's opening
estimates.columns: 'one on each side' by the jambs (40:49), like Solomon's two pillars. Their size is not given, so they are drawn 12 round and 18 high, as Solomon's were (1 Kgs 7:15), without capitals, standing on the court before the portico
estimates.temple-walls: 6 thick (41:5), with the nave's doorway 10 wide (41:2); the doorway is drawn 15 high, which is not given. The house's height is not given either; it is drawn 30, as Solomon's was (1 Kgs 6:2), the walls stepping in a cubit at each storey of the side rooms (41:6-7)
estimates.partition: jambs 2 thick either side of a doorway 6 wide (41:3); the doorway is drawn 10 high, which is not given
estimates.side-rooms: 4 wide (41:5), in three storeys of thirty rooms (41:6), inside an outer wall 5 thick (41:9). The storeys' height is not given; they are drawn 5 cubits each, as Solomon's were (1 Kgs 6:10). The rooms' partitions are not drawn
estimates.side-floors: the rooms widen at each level as the wall narrows (41:6-7): drawn as floors resting on the wall's ledges, so the rooms are 4, 5 and 6 cubits wide. The floors are assumed to be a cubit thick
estimates.stairway: 'a stairway went up from the lowest story to the highest, through the middle one' (41:7). Its form and place are not given; it is drawn winding, in the north rooms
estimates.platform: 'the full length of a rod, six long cubits' (41:8), taken as its height. It is drawn under the house and side rooms, with the 5-cubit open area round them (41:11) on top of it
estimates.side-doors: one on the north and one on the south (41:11); their place along the wall is not given
estimates.west-building: 70 wide and 90 long inside walls 5 thick (41:12), across the yard behind the temple. Its west wall is taken to be the outer wall's, so it is drawn 74 cubits deep rather than 80. Its height and roof are not given
estimates.panelling: 'paneled from the ground to the windows' (41:16); drawn from floor to ceiling. The carved cherubim and palm trees of 41:17-20 are not drawn
estimates.temple-windows: 'beveled windows' (41:16); their number and size are not given. Drawn as slots high in the walls, above the side rooms, as in Solomon's temple
estimates.wooden-altar: 3 high and 2 long (41:22); the BSB's 'square' assumes its width. Where it stood is not given; it is drawn in the nave before the inner sanctuary, where the tabernacle's incense altar stood (Exod 30:6)
estimates.doors: two panels to each door (41:23-24), filling the doorways; drawn closed
estimates.canopy: 'a wooden canopy outside, on the front of the portico' (41:25). The Hebrew is uncertain (JPS: 'a lattice of wood'). Drawn as an overhang above the portico's opening
estimates.roof: Ezekiel does not describe the house's roof. 'The side rooms of the temple also had canopies' (41:26) is the nearest, so the roofs go on there. They are drawn flat, in wood
estimates.north-chambers: 100 × 50 (42:2), in three storeys with the upper ones set back (42:5-6), with a walkway 10 wide in front (42:4). The rooms on the outer court are 50 long and those facing the temple 100 (42:8). This is drawn as two rows 20 deep either side of the walkway, the shorter one at the west end, which is one common reading. The storeys are drawn 5 high; neither depth nor height is given
estimates.north-chamber-wall: 'an outer wall in front of the chambers… fifty cubits long' (42:7), drawn where the outer row is short. Its height and thickness are not given
estimates.south-chambers: 'the same length and width' as the north chambers (42:11), with a wall like theirs (42:12)
estimates.altar-base: a gutter a cubit deep and a cubit wide, with a rim of a span round its edge (43:13, 17). The base is drawn 18 square: the 16 of the lower ledge with a cubit of gutter either side. The span is taken as half a cubit
estimates.altar-ledges: 2 cubits up to the lower ledge and 4 more to the larger one, each ledge a cubit wide (43:14). The larger is 14 square (43:17). The lower's 16 is worked out from the ledges' width, not stated
estimates.altar-horns: 'four horns shall project upward from the hearth' (43:15); their size is not given
estimates.altar-steps: 'the steps of the altar shall face east' (43:17). Their number and size are not given; a flight of eleven is drawn up to the larger ledge, from which the hearth is served

title: A fishing boat of the Sea of Galilee
summary: The kind of boat the Gospels' fishermen worked from, and the one Jesus slept in 'in the stern, on the cushion' (Mark 4:38) while the storm swamped it. In 1986, with the lake at a low ebb, a hull of the period was found in the mud near Ginosar. It is about 8.2 m long and 2.3 m across, and 1.2 m of its height survives. Pottery found with it runs from the late 1st century BC to about AD 70, and radiocarbon dates its wood to 40 BC ± 80 years. Nothing ties it to Jesus or the disciples; it is a boat of their time and lake. The model follows the surviving hull: a rounded stern, a fine bow, cedar planks edge-joined with pegged mortise-and-tenon joints on a keel, and oak frames. It had been repaired many times, and besides the cedar and oak it holds single pieces of five other woods. Everything above the hull is reconstructed: the decks at bow and stern, the rowers' benches, the mast (nail holes on the keel show where its step was fastened), the sail, four oars and the steering oars. Josephus puts four sailors in each boat, and a helmsman, so a crew of five. Wachsmann estimates fifteen men could fit in a boat this size, enough for Jesus and the Twelve. Each estimate says what it rests on, in the list under the model.
dimensions: ≈ 8.2 × 2.3 m · 1.2 m of its height survives

estimates.planks: the length, beam and shape are the surviving hull's. Its sides are broken off at about 1.2 m, and the sheer (the top edge of the sides) is drawn a little above that, rising towards the ends; how high it was is not known. The strakes are drawn as even bands, not plank by plank
estimates.frames: oak, as found, but drawn every 0.3 m as even ribs; the spacing and the many repairs of the surviving frames are not followed
estimates.stern-deck: 'both the fore and aft sections were probably decked in, although the boat was not preserved to this height' (Wachsmann, 1988). The deck's size is not known
estimates.bow-deck: as the stern deck: probable, but not preserved
estimates.benches: not preserved. Two benches are drawn for four rowers, after Josephus's four sailors to a boat
estimates.wales: not preserved; a heavier timber along the top of each side is drawn for the oars to bear on
estimates.mast: only the nail holes where the mast step was fastened to the keel survive, a little forward of amidships. The mast's height and the yard's length are not known; they are drawn at ≈6 m and ≈3.4 m
estimates.sail: a single square sail, drawn brailed up to the yard (furled) as it would be under oars or in a storm. The hull shows only that it had a mast; the sail's shape and size are the reconstruction's
estimates.oars: four, two a side, for Josephus's four sailors; the Migdal mosaic, of a boat of this period, shows three a side, the sternmost a steering oar. Their length (≈4 m) is not known
estimates.steering-oars: one on each quarter, as in the museum's reconstruction; the Migdal mosaic shows its sternmost oar widening into a steering oar. Their size is not known
estimates.cushion: Mark 4:38's proskephalaion, 'the cushion', with the article, as if it belonged to the boat. Wachsmann suggests a sandbag of the kind kept as ballast, stowed under the stern deck, and it is drawn there. Its size and shape are not known

title: Goliath's armour — as 1 Samuel 17 describes it
summary: Read or play 1 Samuel 17:4–7 and the Philistine champion is armed as the text lists it: his height, then the bronze helmet and the coat of scale armour, then the bronze greaves and the javelin between his shoulders, and last the spear and the shield-bearer who walked before him. Elsewhere he is shown whole, with the sword David later drew from its sheath (17:51). The text gives two weights. The coat weighs 5,000 shekels (≈57 kg) and the spear's iron point 600 shekels (≈6.8 kg), converted on a shekel of ≈11.4 g as in the BSB's notes; the model sizes the point to that weight. His height is where the witnesses differ. The Masoretic text, which the BSB follows, has 'six cubits and a span' (≈2.9 m on a common cubit of ≈44.5 cm); the Dead Sea scroll 4QSamᵃ (1st century BC), Codex Vaticanus and the Lucianic Greek, and Josephus have 'four cubits and a span' (≈2.0 m). He is drawn at the Masoretic height, with the ordinary figure's proportions, and the size figure (≈1.66 m) stands where his shield-bearer went before him. The shapes of the pieces, the length of the spear and javelin, the shield and the sword are reconstructed; each says what it rests on, both at the step that adds it and in the list under the model. The text does not say whose pattern the armour follows. Scholars point out that it does not match the Philistines on the Egyptian reliefs of the 12th century BC. They have read it as Near Eastern scale armour, as the Greek panoply of helmet, scale corselet, greaves and a great shield with a bearer, or as a mixture drawn from several.
dimensions: 6 cubits and a span · ≈ 2.9 m (MT); 4 cubits and a span · ≈ 2.0 m (4QSamᵃ, LXX, Josephus)

omits.sword: vv. 4-7 do not mention it; he comes with 'sword and spear and javelin' (v. 45), and David draws it from its sheath (v. 51)

estimates.goliath: six cubits and a span, the Masoretic reading the BSB follows; the span is taken as half a cubit, so ≈ 2.9 m on the common cubit (the BSB's note, on a longer cubit, gives 297 cm). 4QSamᵃ, the oldest Hebrew witness to the verse, Codex Vaticanus, the Lucianic Greek and Josephus (Ant. 6.9.1) read four cubits and a span, ≈ 2.0 m. Hays (2005) argues for the shorter reading, Billington (2007) for the taller. His build is the ordinary figure's, scaled to his height; the text says nothing of it
estimates.helmet: the text says only that it was bronze (kova, Strong's 'a helmet (as arched)'). Drawn as a rounded cap with a rolled rim. Its shape is not known; it is not the feathered headdress the Philistines wear on the Egyptian reliefs at Medinet Habu (A. Yadin 2004, after Galling)
estimates.coat-of-mail: shiryon qasqassim, a corslet 'of scales', the word used of a fish's scales (Lev 11:9), so it is drawn as bronze scale armour. The text gives its weight, 5,000 shekels (≈ 57 kg), not its cut or length; it is drawn from the neck to mid-thigh with sleeves to the elbow, and the scales are a pattern, not counted pieces
estimates.greaves: mitschot, 'a shinpiece of armour', only here in the Bible; bronze, 'on his legs'. Drawn from the ankle to below the knee, wrapping the shin and open behind the calf. Their shape is not given
estimates.javelin: kidon, 'of bronze… between his shoulders'. The BSB reads a javelin, drawn ≈ 4 cubits (≈ 1.9 m) long, slung across the back with its head over the right shoulder; its length and how it was slung are not given. Strong's glosses it 'a dart'; the KJV has 'a target' (a small shield), and G. Molin (1956) took it to be a curved sword, a scimitar. Only the head is taken to be bronze; the shaft is drawn in wood
estimates.spear-shaft: 'like a weaver's beam', the beam of a loom, and so taken as thick: drawn ≈ 6 cm across and 7 cubits (≈ 3.1 m) long, neither of which is given. Y. Yadin (1955) read the likeness as a spear with a loop of cord for throwing, like the leash rods of a loom; it is drawn plain. The same phrase is used of his brother's spear (2 Sam 21:19; 1 Chr 20:5) and of an Egyptian's (1 Chr 11:23)
estimates.spear-point: iron, 600 shekels (≈ 6.8 kg). Its shape is not given. Drawn as a leaf blade ≈ 50 cm long and 14.5 cm wide, ≈ 3.6 cm thick at the middle, on a socket 15 cm long: at 7.9 g/cm³ this holds ≈ 6.9 kg of iron (derived from the model's own shape, not a find)
estimates.shield: a tsinnah, 'a (large) shield', carried by a bearer who went before him (v. 7, v. 41); its size, shape and material are not given. Drawn as a board of hide on a wooden frame ≈ 1.6 × 2.7 cubits (≈ 0.7 × 1.2 m), held before the bearer. The size figure stands where the bearer went; nothing is known of him
estimates.sword: not in vv. 4-7. David draws it 'from its sheath' (17:51); later it lies at Nob wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod, and David says 'there is none like it' (21:9). Its size and shape are not given; it is drawn sheathed at the left hip, ≈ 2 cubits (≈ 0.9 m) long, on a belt

title: Nebuchadnezzar's golden statue — sixty cubits by six
summary: The statue Nebuchadnezzar set up on the plain of Dura for all his officials to bow down to (Daniel 3). The text gives three things: it was gold, sixty cubits high and six cubits wide (≈ 26.7 × 2.7 m on a common cubit of ≈ 44.5 cm; the BSB's note, on a longer cubit, gives 27.4 × 2.7 m). It does not say whom it showed. Many since Hippolytus and Jerome have taken it to be the king himself, but 3:12, 14 and 18 set worshipping it beside serving his gods. As a human figure, sixty by six is ten times as tall as it is wide, where a body is five or six times (Montgomery 1927). Commentators have answered this in two ways. The height may include a pedestal, or the statue may have been a stele carved with a figure only at the top; the Aramaic word, tselem, is used of such a stele at Nerab. The model takes the first reading: a robed figure 30 cubits high on a brick pedestal of 30, the two together 60, and neither wider than 6. The split between them is a choice, not a measurement. 'Gold' is taken, as in Isaiah 40:19 and Jeremiah 10:4, to be gold plating on a core; the model shows only the gold surface. The figure's long robe, beard and tall banded crown follow how Babylonian gods and kings are shown, not any known statue. Each of these choices is listed under the model with what it rests on. The sixty and the six are sexagesimal, Babylon's way of counting, as is Ezekiel's rod of six cubits (Ezek 40:5). For scale, Herodotus reports a figure of solid gold twelve cubits high in the temple of Bel at Babylon, and Diodorus a hammered-gold statue forty feet high on top of it.

estimates.pedestal: the text gives one height, sixty cubits, for 'the statue'. It is taken here to include a pedestal, as many commentators have suggested, since a figure of human proportions six cubits wide would be 30–36 cubits high (Montgomery 1927: 'as 5 or 6 to 1'). The pedestal is drawn 30 cubits high and six square, of baked brick, Babylon's building material; its height, shape and material are not given. J. Oppert took a brick mass near Babylon, 14 m square and 6 m high, to be the pedestal (Expédition scientifique en Mésopotamie, 1863, cited by Montgomery). That mass is much wider than six cubits, and the place of Dura is not certainly known
estimates.statue: gold, 'sixty cubits high and six cubits wide' with the pedestal (see the pedestal). The figure is drawn 30 cubits high, standing, and at most 5.8 cubits across at the shoulders. It is taken to be wood or another core plated with gold, as idols are in Isa 40:19, Jer 10:3-4 and the Letter of Jeremiah; only the gold is drawn. The text does not say whom it depicts. The long robe, the squared beard, the arms at the sides and the tall crown with bands follow Babylonian images of gods and kings in general, such as Marduk on the lapis seal of Marduk-zākir-šumi I (Berlin, VA Bab 646). No statue of this kind survives to copy
